title: Cognitive Architecture and Instructional Design: 20 Years Later

findings.antecedent: conventional problems (requiring means-ends analysis)
findings.mechanism: means-ends analysis is exceptionally expensive of working memory capacity
findings.quote: conventional problems (...) are typically solved by means-ends analysis, a process that is exceptionally expensive of working memory capacity

findings.antecedent: goal-free problems (non-specific goal)
findings.mechanism: learners are no longer able to extract differences between a current problem state and a goal state simply because no goal state is provided
findings.quote: goal-free problem solving greatly reduces cognitive load and provides precisely the combination of low load

findings.antecedent: goal-free problems (non-specific goal)
findings.mechanism: provides precisely the combination of low load and focus on solutions that is required for knowledge construction
findings.quote: goal-free problem solving greatly reduces cognitive load and provides precisely the combination of low load and focus on solutions that is required for knowledge construction.

findings.antecedent: worked examples (full problem solution)
findings.mechanism: focus the learners' attention on problem states and associated operators (i.e. solution steps)
findings.quote: Worked examples aim to reduce the cognitive load caused by conventional problems and to facilitate knowledge construction.

findings.antecedent: worked examples (full problem solution)
findings.consequent: knowledge construction and transfer performance (compared to conventional problems)
findings.mechanism: focus the learners' attention on problem states and associated operators (i.e. solution steps), enabling them to induce generalised solutions.
findings.quote: studying worked examples may facilitate knowledge construction and transfer performance more than actually solving the equivalent problems.

findings.antecedent: completion problems (partial solution)
findings.consequent: learner study and understanding of examples
findings.mechanism: learners must carefully study and understand the partial worked examples provided in completion problems because they otherwise will not be able to complete the solution correctly.
findings.quote: learners must carefully study and understand the partial worked examples provided in completion problems because they otherwise will not be able to complete the solution correctly.

findings.antecedent: multiple, spatially separated sources of complementary information (e.g., diagram and solution statements)
findings.mechanism: learners must mentally integrate the two sources of information in order to understand the solution
findings.quote: Learners must mentally integrate the two sources of information in order to understand the solution, a process that yields a high cognitive load and hampers learning.

findings.antecedent: physically integrating spatially separated sources of complementary information
findings.mechanism: making mental integration superfluous
findings.quote: This split-attention effect can be prevented by physically integrating the diagram and the solution statements, making mental integration superfluous

findings.antecedent: temporally coordinated animation and associated narration
findings.mechanism: to decrease cognitive load and facilitate learning
findings.quote: Mayer and Anderson (1992) found that animation and associated narration need to be temporally coordinated in order to decrease cognitive load and facilitate learning.

findings.antecedent: two self-contained sources of identical information presented together (e.g., diagram and text)
findings.mechanism: effortful processing is required from the learners to eventually discover that the information from the two sources is identical.
findings.quote: It was found that only presenting the diagram was superior to presenting both sources of information together.

findings.antecedent: using both visual and auditory working memory (e.g., diagram with spoken text)
findings.mechanism: working memory can be subdivided into partially independent processors, one dealing with verbal materials based on an auditory working memory and one dealing with diagrammatic/pictorial information based on a visual working memory
findings.quote: effective working memory capacity can be increased by using both visual and auditory working memory rather than either processor alone.

findings.antecedent: high variability over problem situations
findings.mechanism: increases the probability that similar features can be identified and that relevant features can be distinguished from irrelevant ones.
findings.quote: increases in variability increase intrinsic cognitive load allowing more to be learned provided there is sufficient working memory resources to handle the increase.

findings.antecedent: high variability over problem situations (under low total cognitive load)
findings.mechanism: increases the probability that similar features can be identified and that relevant features can be distinguished from irrelevant ones.
findings.quote: high variability would have a positive effect on learning and transfer in situations in which cognitive load was low

findings.antecedent: high variability over problem situations (under high total cognitive load)
findings.mechanism: the total cognitive load would then overburden learners' working memory
findings.quote: high variability would have a negative effect on learning and transfer in situations in which cognitive load was already high

findings.antecedent: worked examples combined with self-explanation prompts
findings.mechanism: elicit sophisticated self-explanations from the learners
findings.quote: Several studies showed that worked examples combined with self-explanation prompts can be superior to worked examples without self-explanation prompts

findings.antecedent: learners asked to imagine or mentally rehearse a concept or process (with increased knowledge)
findings.mechanism: With increased knowledge, working memory limits expand and so imagining the material becomes increasingly feasible because it can be more readily processed in working memory.
findings.quote: Once information can be adequately imagined, imagination instructions are superior to study instructions

findings.antecedent: novices asked to imagine or mentally rehearse a concept or process
findings.mechanism: Novices in a given area may be unable to adequately process high element interactivity information because of working memory limits when dealing with novel information.
findings.quote: For such learners, imagination may be difficult or impossible and so studying the information results in enhanced learning compared to imagining the same information.

findings.antecedent: presenting individual elements of high element interactivity information sequentially, then fully integrated information
findings.mechanism: individual elements were learned first without learning the interactions between them. Once the individual elements are stored in long-term memory, it may be feasible to subsequently integrate the elements by learning the interactions between them.
findings.quote: Results supported this hypothesis. Learners presented all of the information twice were unable to process it properly on either occasion due to an excessive working memory load.

findings.antecedent: instructional procedures designed for novices (e.g., worked examples)
findings.mechanism: With increases in expertise, element interactivity decreases due to the environmental organising and linking principle.
findings.quote: Instructional procedures designed for novices dealing with multiple, interacting elements can be counterproductive as expertise increases

findings.antecedent: additional information or activities (e.g., studying worked examples) for experts
findings.mechanism: With increases in expertise, these same activities may become redundant and impose an unnecessary cognitive load.
findings.quote: With increases in expertise, these same activities may become redundant and impose an unnecessary cognitive load.

findings.antecedent: collaborative learning for tasks imposing high cognitive load
findings.mechanism: benefits of dividing information processing among group members proved to be higher than the transaction costs.
findings.quote: learning from tasks imposing a high cognitive load led to more efficient collaborative learning

findings.antecedent: collaborative learning for tasks imposing low cognitive load
findings.mechanism: inter-individual communication and coordination of information were unnecessary and resulted in transaction costs that were higher than the benefits of distributing the cognitive load
findings.quote: when cognitive load was low, qualitative differences in constructed knowledge materialised in higher learning efficiency for those who learned individually than for those who learned collaboratively.

findings.antecedent: transient information (e.g., spoken text, animation) that disappears quickly
findings.mechanism: it may be necessary for the learner to actively retain information in working memory for later processing
findings.quote: it may be necessary for the learner to actively retain information in working memory for later processing which increases extraneous cognitive load

findings.antecedent: transient information (e.g., spoken text, animation) that disappears quickly
findings.mechanism: increases extraneous cognitive load and so reduces learning
findings.quote: increases extraneous cognitive load and so reduces learning.

findings.antecedent: learner control over the pace of an instructional animation (self-pacing)
findings.mechanism: helps them deal with the transient nature of this information
findings.quote: Mayer and Chandler (2001), who found that it was beneficial to give learners control over the pace of an instructional animation

findings.antecedent: segmented animations (with pauses in between) for novice learners
findings.mechanism: helps them deal with the transient nature of this information
findings.quote: segmented animations (i.e. segmented in parts with pauses in between) were more efficient than continuous animations for novice learners

findings.antecedent: short pieces of audio-visual information
findings.mechanism: interaction effect of transient information on the modality effect
findings.quote: short pieces of audio-visual information were more effective than visual information only

findings.antecedent: longer pieces of audio-visual information
findings.mechanism: abundance of transient information in the longer, auditory piece
findings.quote: longer pieces of audio-visual information were less effective than visual information only because of the abundance of transient information in the longer, auditory piece.

findings.antecedent: students taught to apply CLT principles to self-manage cognitive load (with badly designed materials)
findings.consequent: performance on recall and transfer tests
findings.mechanism: better equipped to deal with these badly designed materials
findings.quote: superior performance of the students in the self-management condition on recall and transfer tests.

findings.antecedent: animation (compared to statics) to teach cognitive tasks involving human movement
findings.mechanism: humans have evolved the ability to learn from observing others engage in action and copy it effortlessly.
findings.quote: it is better to use animation rather than statics to teach cognitive tasks involving human movement.

findings.antecedent: finger tracing angle relationships when studying worked examples
findings.mechanism: making movements, such as gestures and tracing, can affect available working memory resources and cognitive load.
findings.quote: Hu et al. (2015) showed that students who traced angle relationships with their index finger when studying paper-based worked examples in geometry showed higher learning outcomes

findings.antecedent: making gestures during problem-solving
findings.mechanism: making gestures can be used for cognitive offloading of information during problem-solving
findings.quote: making gestures can be used for cognitive offloading of information during problem-solving, leading to a reduction in working memory load

findings.antecedent: massed presentations of information
findings.mechanism: Massed practice may reduce working memory resources while spaced practice may allow resources to recover.
findings.quote: massed presentations resulted in a reduced working memory capacity compared to spaced presentations.

findings.antecedent: stress, emotions, and uncertainty (as extraneous load)
findings.mechanism: may restrict the capacity of working memory by competing with task-relevant processes
findings.quote: stress, emotions and uncertainty may restrict the capacity of working memory by competing with task-relevant processes; thus, they increase cognitive load

findings.antecedent: stress, emotions, and uncertainty (as extraneous load)
findings.mechanism: may restrict the capacity of working memory by competing with task-relevant processes; thus, they increase cognitive load, hamper learning and decrease transfer
findings.quote: stress, emotions and uncertainty may restrict the capacity of working memory by competing with task-relevant processes; thus, they increase cognitive load, hamper learning and decrease transfer

findings.antecedent: stress, emotions, and uncertainty (as integral elements of the task)
findings.mechanism: if emotion, stress and uncertainty are seen as an integral element of the task that must be learned, they contribute to intrinsic cognitive load
findings.quote: if emotion, stress and uncertainty are seen as an integral element of the task that must be learned, they contribute to intrinsic cognitive load

findings.antecedent: learners
findings.quote: A general finding is that learners are not good in regulating their learning (Bjork et al. 2013).

findings.antecedent: ease of processing (e.g., text is easily read)
findings.consequent: learners' judgment of understanding and future performance
findings.mechanism: students often use ‘ease of processing' as a cue for understanding and future performance
findings.quote: students often use ‘ease of processing' as a cue for understanding and future performance: if a text is easily read, students typically judge their understanding of the text and their performance on a future test as high.

findings.antecedent: high cognitive load (e.g., from means-ends analysis)
findings.mechanism: a learner (...) may use the high cognitive load as an invalid cue for learning (‘this cost me a lot of effort so I must have learned a lot')
findings.quote: a learner who is solving a conventional problem using means-ends-analysis may use the high cognitive load as an invalid cue for learning

tables.description: Timeline of major cognitive load effects before and after 1998, including effect name, first publication, and description.

limitations: Current knowledge is incomplete, and future research is needed to continue development.
The assumption of fixed working memory capacity in CLT might be untenable, as working memory resource depletion occurs.
Current understanding of self-regulated learning and the interaction of primary and secondary knowledge needs rethinking for teaching.
CLT does not fully address how physical environments evoking stress, emotions, and uncertainty affect cognitive load.
The special role of human movement in working memory might require reconsideration of human cognitive architecture.
There is virtually no evidence that self-regulation is teachable as a domain-general procedure.
More research is needed into objective measurement techniques for cognitive load and their potential.
